facts.text: Richard Marshal, Earl of Pembroke, was defeated by knights loyal to King Henry III of England at the Battle of the Curragh in County Kildare, Ireland.
Robert Winchelsey left England for Rome to be consecrated Archbishop of Canterbury, but a papal vacancy delayed the ceremony.
A band of warriors led by Niels Ebbesen killed Count Gerhard III, ending Holstein rule in Denmark.
Mexican Texans met at San Felipe de Austin to begin the Convention of 1833.
American Civil War: The Union Army under Major General Philip Sheridan inflicted more than 2,900 casualties on the Confederates at the Battle of Five Forks.

image.caption: Date April 1, 1865 ( 1865-04-01 ) Location Five Forks, Dinwiddie County, Virginia 37°08′22″N 77°37′22″W ﻿ / ﻿ 37.13944°N 77.62278°W ﻿ / 37.13944; -77.62278 Result Union victory

facts.text: The Duke of Buckingham opened the first section of the Brill Tramway, a short railway line to transport goods between his lands and the national rail network.

links.title: Richard Temple-Nugent-Brydges-Chandos-Grenville, 3rd Duke of Buckingham and Chandos

facts.text: The Inland Customs Line, established by the British for the collection of the salt tax in India, was abandoned.

links.title: History of the salt tax in British India

facts.text: The United Kingdom established the Royal Air Force, near the end of the First World War.
English cricketer Wally Hammond set a record for the highest individual score in Test cricket of 336 not out during a match against New Zealand.
Soviet border guards opened fire on civilians attempting to cross the border from the Soviet Union to Romania near Fântâna Albă, killing between 44 and 3,000 people.
Israel enacted a citizenship law, prior to which the country technically had no citizens.
The British Army's Mobile Defence Corps, intended to assist with civil defence after a nuclear attack, was established by royal warrant.
On Her Majesty's Secret Service, the tenth novel of Ian Fleming 's James Bond series, was released in the United Kingdom.

links.title: List of James Bond novels and short stories

facts.text: The Hawker Siddeley Harrier, the first operational fighter aircraft with V/STOL capabilities, entered service with the Royal Air Force.
U.S. president Richard Nixon signed the Public Health Cigarette Smoking Act into law, requiring that a prominent warning by the surgeon general be placed on cigarette packages.

links.title: Surgeon General of the United States

facts.text: The American Motors Corporation introduced its Gremlin, promoted as America's first subcompact car.
The longest prison riot in British penal history began at Strangeways Prison in Manchester, lasting 25 days.
Same-sex marriage in the Netherlands was legalized, making it the first country to do so.
Hundred Years' War: John, Duke of Normandy, laid siege to the town of Aiguillon.
Under the South Seas Mandate, Japan set up a government in Koror, precipitating large-scale Japanese settlement in Palau.
Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak founded Apple Computer, Inc..

image.caption: Born ( 1955-02-24 ) February 24, 1955 San Francisco, California, U.S.

facts.text: An American Lockheed EP-3 and a Chinese Shenyang J-8 collided in mid-air off Hainan, resulting in an international dispute between the two countries.
The first modern Italian Parliament is opened in Turin, following the annexation of Central Italy into the Kingdom of Sardinia.
American Civil War: On the third attempt, Union forces captured Petersburg, Virginia, although Confederate officials and most of their remaining troops were able to escape.
2001: A Space Odyssey, the epic science fiction film produced and directed by Stanley Kubrick, premiered at the Uptown Theater in Washington, D.C.
Spores of anthrax were accidentally released from a military research facility near the city of Sverdlovsk, causing at least 68 deaths.
Argentine special forces invaded the Falkland Islands, sparking the Falklands War against the United Kingdom.
Bosnian War: At least 48 civilians were massacred in the town of Bijeljina in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

John Gotti, the head of the Gambino crime family of New York City, was convicted of racketeering, murder, conspiracy to commit murder, loansharking, obstruction of justice, illegal gambling, and tax evasion.

links.title: Obstruction of justice in the United States

facts.text: Second Intifada: Palestinian militants sought refuge from advancing Israeli forces in the Church of the Nativity in Bethlehem, beginning a month-long siege.

links.title: Siege of the Church of the Nativity

facts.text: A gunman shot at people inside Oikos University, a Korean Christian college in Oakland, California, leaving seven people dead and three injured.
Six elderly men burgled a safe-deposit facility in Hatton Garden, London, and stole items worth up to an estimated £14 million.
Spanish conquistador Juan Ponce de León sighted land in North America, naming the area La Florida.
Creatures of Impulse, by W. S. Gilbert, premiered at the Court Theatre in London.
The Australian Bureau of Statistics conducted the first national census of the country.
Gunmen attacked Garissa University College in Kenya, killing 148 people and wounding 79 others.
Edward the Confessor, usually considered to be the last king of the House of Wessex, was crowned King of England.
Robert Walpole took office as First Lord of the Treasury, Chancellor of the Exchequer and Leader of the House of Commons, becoming the first de facto prime minister of Great Britain.

links.title: Leader of the House of Commons
Prime Minister of the United Kingdom

facts.text: The Pony Express, a mail service that became the most direct means of long-distance communication across the United States before the first transcontinental telegraph, began operation.
The libel trial instigated by Irish author Oscar Wilde began, eventually resulting in his arrest, trial and imprisonment on charges of gross indecency.

image.caption: Born Oscar Fingal O'Fflahertie Wills Wilde ( 1854-10-16 ) 16 October 1854 Dublin , Ireland

facts.text: Joseph Stalin became the first general secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union.

links.title: General Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union

facts.text: Lord Clydesdale and David McIntyre undertook the first successful flight over Mount Everest.
Philippine resistance against Japan: Cebuano fishermen discovered the Koga papers after a plane crash killed Admiral Mineichi Koga, commander-in-chief of the Imperial Japanese Navy 's Combined Fleet.
The Marshall Plan, an economic recovery program established by U.S. Secretary of State George Marshall to assist the post- World War II re-building of Europe, was signed into law.
The Super Outbreak of 148 tornadoes began, killing at least 315 people and injuring 5,484 in 13 US states at the end of a very strong La Niña event.
Aboard Soyuz T-11, Rakesh Sharma became the first Indian to be launched into space.
A U.S. Air Force CT-43 crashed into a mountainside while attempting an instrument approach to Dubrovnik Airport in Croatia, killing all 35 people on board, including Secretary of Commerce Ron Brown.
In United States v. Microsoft Corp., Microsoft was found to have violated antitrust law by bundling the web browser Internet Explorer with its Windows operating system.
Texas law enforcement authorities raided the Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints ' YFZ Ranch, eventually removing 533 women and children from the premises.

links.title: Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints

facts.text: A gunman opened fire at the American Civic Association in Binghamton, New York, U.S., killing thirteen and wounding four before committing suicide.
Apple Inc. released the first generation iPad, a tablet computer.
The northeastern section of Buenos Aires Province, Argentina, experienced several flash floods that killed at least 100 people.
Henry II of France and Philip II of Spain signed the second treaty of Cateau-Cambrésis, ending the Italian War of 1551–1559.
Emma Elizabeth Smith was killed in the first of eleven unsolved murders of women that took place in or near the impoverished Whitechapel district in the East End of London.
Luna 10 entered orbit around the Moon, becoming the first space probe to orbit an astronomical body other than Earth or the Sun.
A woman opened fire at YouTube headquarters in San Bruno, California, injuring three people before killing herself.
The Komnenos dynasty came to full power with the coronation of Alexios I Komnenos as Byzantine emperor.

image.caption: Byzantine emperor

links.title: Byzantine Empire under the Komnenos dynasty

facts.text: Napoleon abdicated as Emperor of the French and named his son Napoleon II to replace him.

William Henry Harrison became the first U.S. president to die in office, sparking a brief constitutional crisis regarding questions of presidential succession that were unanswered by the U.S. Constitution.

links.title: United States presidential line of succession

facts.text: The Kennel Club, the world's oldest kennel club, was founded in the United Kingdom after Sewallis Shirley became frustrated by trying to organise dog shows without a consistent set of rules.
Bryant's Minstrels premiered the minstrel song " Dixie " in New York City as part of their blackface show.
An earthquake hit the Kangra Valley in India, killing at least 20,000 people and destroying 100,000 buildings.

Twelve nations signed the North Atlantic Treaty, establishing NATO, an international military alliance whereby its member states agree to mutual defense in response to an attack by any external party.
American civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr. was assassinated in Memphis, Tennessee.

image.caption: Location 35°08′04″N 90°03′27″W ﻿ / ﻿ 35.1345°N 90.0576°W ﻿ / 35.1345; -90.0576 Lorraine Motel Memphis, Tennessee , U.S.

links.title: Assassination of Martin Luther King Jr.

facts.text: A year after the completion of the second of the complex's twin towers, the World Trade Center in New York City was officially dedicated.

links.title: Construction of the World Trade Center

facts.text: A C-141, dubbed the Hanoi Taxi, flew the last mission of Operation Homecoming to return American prisoners of war from Vietnam.
Bill Gates and Paul Allen founded Microsoft in Albuquerque, New Mexico, to develop and sell BASIC interpreters for the Altair 8800.
Vietnam War: On a mission to evacuate children from South Vietnam, a U.S. Air Force plane crash-landed at Tan Son Nhut Air Base, killing 78 children and 60 others.
Evan Mecham, Governor of Arizona, was removed from office after being convicted in his impeachment trial.
A building collapsed on tribal land in Thane in Maharashtra, India, causing 74 deaths.
The Byzantine Empire and the Republic of Venice signed a five-year peace treaty.
Queen Elizabeth I knighted Francis Drake for completing a circumnavigation of the world.
The current flag of Hong Kong was adopted for post-colonial use during the Third Session of the Seventh National People's Congress.

image.caption: Use Civil and state flag , civil and state ensign

facts.text: Georgian Airways Flight 834 crashed at N'djili Airport in Kinshasa, killing 32 people and leaving one survivor.
The Fatimid Caliphate began a second unsuccessful invasion of Egypt, then under Abbasid rule.

Northern Crusades: In the Battle on the Ice, Novgorod forces led by Alexander Nevsky rebuffed an invasion attempt by the Teutonic Knights at Lake Peipus on the present-day border of Estonia and Russia.
Pocahontas, a Native American woman, married English colonist John Rolfe, leading to a period of peace between the Powhatan people and the inhabitants of Jamestown, Virginia.

image.caption: Born Amonute c. 1596 [ 1 ] Werowocomoco , Tsenacommacah (near present-day Gloucester Courthouse, Virginia , U.S. )

links.title: Native Americans in the United States

facts.text: Birkenhead Park, generally acknowledged as the world's first publicly funded civic park, opened in Birkenhead, England.
A spectator stand collapsed during a football match at Ibrox Park in Govan, Scotland, killing 25 supporters and injuring more than 500 others.
Nazi sympathisers attempted to kidnap two German-Jewish filmmakers in Liechtenstein.
An F5 tornado struck Tupelo, Mississippi, killing at least 216 people during one of the deadliest tornado outbreaks in U.S. history.
Siegfried Lederer, a Czech Jew, escaped from Auschwitz with the aid of an SS officer who opposed the Holocaust.

links.title: History of the Jews in the Czech lands

facts.text: Aware that he was slowing down both physically and mentally in his old age, Winston Churchill retired as prime minister of the United Kingdom.

links.title: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom

facts.text: During the Buddhist Uprising, South Vietnamese military prime minister Nguyễn Cao Kỳ personally attempted to lead the capture of the restive city of Đà Nẵng before backing down.
Faculty members, clerical workers, and librarians at Boston University went on strike.
The Libyan secret service bombed a discotheque in West Berlin, resulting in three deaths and 229 others injured.
The Akashi Kaikyo Bridge, then the world's longest suspension bridge, linking Awaji Island and Kobe in Japan, opened to traffic.

links.title: List of longest suspension bridge spans

facts.text: Fan violence broke out before a UEFA Cup semifinal in Istanbul, Turkey, resulting in two Leeds United supporters being stabbed to death and Galatasaray supporters being banned from attending the second leg in England.
In the first reported data breach, 250,000 social security numbers collected by the State of California were stolen from a data center.

The North Korean satellite Kwangmyŏngsŏng-2 was launched from the Tonghae Satellite Launching Ground and passed over Japan, sparking concerns it may have been a trial run of technology that could be used to launch intercontinental ballistic missiles.
An explosion at a coal mine in West Virginia killed 29 miners in the United States' worst mining disaster in 40 years.
Agents with the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement raided a slaughterhouse in Tennessee, detaining nearly 100 Hispanic workers in one of the largest immigration raids in the history of the U.S.
The Statute of Anne, the first legislation in Great Britain providing for copyright regulated by the government and courts, received royal assent and entered into force five days later.
Carrie, the first novel by American author Stephen King, was published.

image.caption: Author Stephen King

facts.text: In China, the People's Armed Police, primarily responsible for internal security, was founded.
Two bombings in Pakistan killed up to 50 people and injured around 100 others.
A group of 23 slaves in New York City revolted, setting fire to a building, but were soon recaptured.
Napoleonic Wars: British forces captured the French frigate Niémen in the Bay of Biscay.
Peninsular War: After a three-week siege, the Anglo-Portuguese Army, under the Earl of Wellington, captured Badajoz, Spain, and forced the surrender of the French garrison.
Joseph Smith, Oliver Cowdery, David Whitmer and others formally organized the Church of Christ, starting the Latter Day Saint movement.
John Jacob Astor founded the American Fur Company, the profits from which made him the first multi- millionaire in the United States.
World War II: The Luftwaffe began Operation Retribution, bombing the Yugoslav capital of Belgrade in retaliation for a coup d'état that overthrew the government that had signed the Tripartite Pact.
World War II: German forces invaded Greece and Yugoslavia.
Second World War: The Battle of Slater's Knoll on Bougainville Island concluded with a decisive victory for the Australian Army 's 7th Brigade against the Imperial Japanese Army 's 6th Division.
Four California Highway Patrol officers were killed in a shootout following a traffic stop in Newhall, north of Los Angeles.
ABBA won the Eurovision Song Contest representing Sweden with the song " Waterloo ".
The aircraft carrying Rwandan president Juvénal Habyarimana and Burundian president Cyprien Ntaryamira was shot down in Kigali; the event became the catalyst for the Rwandan genocide.

links.title: Assassination of Juvénal Habyarimana and Cyprien Ntaryamira

facts.text: Lithuanian president Rolandas Paksas became the first European head of state to be removed from office by impeachment.
An earthquake measuring 6.3 M w struck near L'Aquila in the central Italian region of Abruzzo, killing 308 people and leaving more than 66,000 homeless.
Mass protests began across Moldova against the results of the parliamentary election.
Naxalite–Maoist insurgency: Insurgents from the Communist Party of India (Maoist) ambushed a Central Reserve Police Force convoy in Dantewada district, India, killing 76 officers.
The National Movement for the Liberation of Azawad unilaterally declared the region of Azawad independent from Mali.

links.title: National Movement for the Liberation of Azawad

facts.text: A bus carrying the Humboldt Broncos collided with a semi-truck, killing 16 and injuring 13.
Dutch sailor Jan van Riebeeck landed at Table Bay in southern Africa, establishing a settlement that later became known as Cape Town.
American Revolutionary War: Ships of the Continental Navy unsuccessfully attempted to capture HMS Glasgow near Block Island.
Varney Air Lines made its first commercial flight, later forming the basis of United Airlines.

image.caption: A United Boeing 777-300ER

facts.text: Kurdish leader Jalal Talabani was elected by the National Assembly as the first non-Arab president of Iraq.
Mexican drug war: Authorities discovered 59 bodies in clandestine mass graves linked to earlier bus hijackings in San Fernando, Tamaulipas.
After a conclave lasting eighty days, the College of Cardinals elected Fabio Chigi as Pope Alexander VII.
American Civil War: Union forces defeated Confederate troops at the Battle of Shiloh, at the time the bloodiest battle in U.S. history, in Hardin County, Tennessee.
An Arctic expedition led by Norwegian explorer Fridtjof Nansen reached 86°13.6′N, almost three degrees beyond the previous Farthest North latitude.
World War II: U.S. forces sank the Japanese battleship Yamato during Operation Kikusui I in the East China Sea.
The United Nations established the World Health Organization to act as a coordinating authority on international public health.
The Rodgers and Hammerstein musical South Pacific, based on Tales of the South Pacific by James Michener, opened on Broadway.
American Presbyterian minister Bruce W. Klunder was killed by a bulldozer while protesting the construction of a segregated school in Cleveland, Ohio.

links.title: Racial segregation in the United States

facts.text: Communist forces overran the South Vietnamese town of Lộc Ninh.
Uganda–Tanzania War: Tanzanian forces defeated Ugandan troops and their Libyan allies at the Battle of Entebbe, opening the way for an advance on the Ugandan capital, Kampala.
Rwandan Civil War: The Rwandan genocide began a few hours after the assassination of President Juvénal Habyarimana, with hundreds of thousands killed in the following 100 days.

links.title: Assassination of Juvénal Habyarimana and Cyprien Ntaryamira

facts.text: First Chechen War: Russian paramilitary troops began a massacre of hundreds of civilians in Samashki, Chechnya.
A hijacker deliberately drove a truck into crowds along Drottninggatan in Stockholm, Sweden, killing five people.
Pedro II became emperor of the Empire of Brazil.
Italian dictator Benito Mussolini survived an assassination attempt by Irishwoman Violet Gibson.
A FedEx employee tried to hijack Federal Express Flight 705 in a failed suicide attempt.
NASA 's 2001 Mars Odyssey, the longest-surviving continually active spacecraft in orbit around a planet other than Earth, launched from Cape Canaveral.
Roman emperor Caracalla was assassinated near Harran and succeeded by his Praetorian Guard prefect Macrinus.

image.caption: Roman emperor

facts.text: Crusades: The Knights Hospitaller surrendered the Krak des Chevaliers, a castle in present-day Syria, to the army of the Mamluk sultan Baybars.
American Civil War: Late-arriving reinforcements helped Confederate forces rout the Union Army at the Battle of Mansfield.
Longacre Square in Midtown Manhattan was renamed Times Square after the New York Times building.
France and the United Kingdom signed the Entente Cordiale, agreeing to a peaceful coexistence after centuries of intermittent conflict.
American cartoonist Winsor McCay released the silent short film Little Nemo (featured), one of the earliest animated films.
World War I: German naval officer Wilhelm Werner murdered 19 captured crew members of the British cargo ship Torrington by submerging U-55 when they were on deck.
The Australian state of Western Australia voted to secede from the federation, but efforts to implement the result proved to be unsuccessful.
A team of computer scientists and others met to discuss the creation of a common business-oriented programming language, which became COBOL.
World War II: The United States Army Air Forces flew its first mission from India over the Hump (the eastern end of the Himalayas ) to deliver materiel to China.
Otto and Elise Hampel were executed in Berlin for performing acts of resistance against Nazism.

BOAC Flight 712 experienced an engine fire shortly after take-off from London Heathrow, leading to the deaths of five people on board, including flight attendant Jane Harrison, who was posthumously awarded a George Cross for heroism.
The Progress Party was founded in a movie theater in Oslo, Norway.
Abbasid forces decisively defeated the Saffarid emir Ya'qub ibn Laith, forcing the latter to halt his advance into Iraq.
Kiliaen van Rensselaer purchased land near present-day Albany, New York, to establish Rensselaerswyck, which became the most successful patroonship under the Dutch West India Company.
The Venus de Milo, an ancient Greek statue of a woman with its arms missing, was discovered on the island of Milos.
A large explosion on board the MV Dara in the Persian Gulf killed 238 people.
On board Soyuz TMA-12, Yi So-yeon became the first Korean astronaut.
First World War: The Canadian Corps began the first wave of attacks of the Battle of Vimy Ridge in Vimy, France.

After being denied permission to perform at Constitution Hall by the Daughters of the American Revolution, African-American singer Marian Anderson gave an open-air concert on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C.
World War II: During the German invasion of Norway, Vidkun Quisling attempted to seize power in the first coup to be broadcast over radio.
Sixteen white and black men began a two-week journey in the American South, acting in defiance of local laws that enforced segregated seating on public buses.

links.title: Racial segregation in the United States

facts.text: The Glazier–Higgins–Woodward tornadoes killed 181 people and injured 970 others in Texas, Oklahoma, and Kansas.
Palestine war: Fighters from the Zionist paramilitary groups Irgun and Lehi attacked the village of Deir Yassin near Jerusalem, killing more than 100 Palestinian Arabs.
NASA announced the selection of the Mercury Seven, the first astronauts in Project Mercury.
The Boeing 737 took its maiden flight, eventually becoming the most produced commercial passenger jet airliner in the world.
The first EMD F40PH, Amtrak 's most widespread diesel locomotive for many years, entered into service.
Iraqi philosopher Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr and his sister Amina were executed by the regime of Saddam Hussein.

image.caption: Title Grand Ayatollah

facts.text: Iranian filmmaker Morteza Avini was killed by a land mine in Fakkeh while producing a documentary.
Ibrahim Baré Maïnassara, President of Niger, was shot dead by soldiers in Niamey.
Invasion of Iraq: Coalition forces captured Baghdad and the statue of Saddam Hussein in Firdos Square was toppled.
Prince Philip, the consort of Queen Elizabeth II, died at Windsor Castle aged 99.

links.title: Death and funeral of Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh

facts.text: Year of the Five Emperors: Septimius Severus was proclaimed Roman emperor by his troops at Carnuntum in modern-day Austria.
Despite being vastly outnumbered, forces of the Old Swiss Confederacy defeated an Austrian army at the Battle of Näfels.
The German heavy cruiser Admiral Scheer, the most successful capital-ship surface raider of the Second World War, was sunk by British bombers in port in Kiel.
Charles, Prince of Wales, married Camilla Parker Bowles in a civil ceremony at the Windsor Guildhall.

links.title: Wedding of Prince Charles and Camilla Parker Bowles

facts.text: Myanmar civil war: Burmese military and police forces killed at least 82 civilians in the Bago massacre, including people protesting a recent coup d'état.
A Mongol army commanded by Tolui captured the city of Merv in present-day Turkmenistan, allegedly killing more than 1.7 million people.

War of the Austrian Succession: Prussian forces defeated Austrian troops at the Battle of Mollwitz in present-day Małujowice, Poland, cementing Frederick II 's authority over the newly conquered territory of Silesia.
Big Ben, the bell in the Palace of Westminster 's clock tower in London, was cast after the original bell cracked during testing.
Mexican Revolution leader Emiliano Zapata was shot to death near Ciudad Ayala, Morelos.

image.caption: Nicknames El Caudillo del Sur , Attila of the South ('el Atila del Sur'), and "E", Mr. Rebel by Woodrow Wilson

facts.text: The Holocaust: Slovak Jewish prisoners Rudolf Vrba and Alfréd Wetzler escaped from Auschwitz, later publishing a report that became one of the earliest and most detailed descriptions of the camp's mass killings.
The U.S. Navy nuclear submarine USS Thresher (SSN-593) sank with all hands lost during deep-diving tests in the North Atlantic Ocean.
In the deadliest aviation accident in Swiss history, Invicta International Airlines Flight 435 crashed into a hillside near Hochwald, killing 108 people of 145 on board.
First Nagorno-Karabakh War: Dozens of Armenian civilians were massacred in the village of Maraga by Azerbaijani forces.
Napoleonic Wars: The War of the Fifth Coalition began with the Austrian invasion of Bavaria, then a client state of France.
Mount Tambora in Indonesia began the most powerful volcanic eruption in recorded history, killing at least 71,000 people and affecting temperatures worldwide.
The Great Gatsby, a novel by American author F. Scott Fitzgerald, was first published by Scribner's.

image.caption: Author F. Scott Fitzgerald

facts.text: In the midst of business disagreements with his bandmates, Paul McCartney announced his departure from the Beatles.
Scientists from the Event Horizon Telescope project released the first image of the black hole at the center of the galaxy M87.
Mongol invasion of Europe: Mongol forces led by Batu Khan and Subutai defeated the army of King Béla IV at the Battle of Mohi near the river Sajó, a key victory in their first invasion of Hungary.
Italian War of 1542–1546: French and Spanish forces fought a massive pitched battle in the Piedmont region of Italy.
The main treaties of the Peace of Utrecht were signed in Utrecht in the Dutch Republic, helping to end the War of the Spanish Succession.
The Treaty of Fontainebleau was signed, ending the War of the Sixth Coalition and forcing Napoleon to abdicate as ruler of France and sending him into exile on Elba.
The Concertgebouw in Amsterdam, considered one of the world's finest concert halls, was inaugurated.
Blücher, the last armored cruiser built by the Imperial German Navy, was launched.

The cricket pavilion at the Nevill Ground was destroyed in an arson attack that was attributed to militant suffragettes as part of a country-wide campaign co-ordinated by the Women's Social and Political Union.

image.caption: Interactive map of Nevill Ground

facts.text: Paris Peace Conference: Woodrow Wilson overturns Japan's Racial Equality Proposal, stating that unanimous support was required.
Emir Abdullah established the first centralised government in the recently created British protectorate of Transjordan.
Pope John XXIII issued Pacem in terris, the first papal encyclical addressed to "all men of good will" rather than only to Catholics.
Rudi Dutschke, the most prominent leader of the German student movement, survived an assassination attempt, which led to the largest protests to that date in Germany.
On the Art of the Cinema, a treatise on film propaganda in support of the ruling Workers' Party of Korea written by the future North Korean leader Kim Jong Il, was published.

links.title: On the Art of the Cinema

facts.text: Uganda–Tanzania War: The allied forces of Tanzania and the Uganda National Liberation Front captured the capital Kampala, deposing Ugandan president Idi Amin.
Prisoners at the Southern Ohio Correctional Facility near Lucasville, Ohio, rioted and took over the prison for 11 days, resulting in the deaths of one officer and nine inmates.

While attempting to set a record as the youngest person to pilot an airplane across the United States, the aircraft flown by seven-year-old Jessica Dubroff crashed in Cheyenne, Wyoming, killing her and two others.
In a coup attempt, members of the Venezuelan military detained President Hugo Chávez and demanded his resignation.
A bomb exploded at the central Oktyabrskaya station of the Minsk Metro in Belarus, killing 15 people and injuring more than 200.
The tour bus of the German football team Borussia Dortmund was attacked with roadside bombs in Dortmund, killing a police officer and injuring one of the team's players.
A Myanmar Air Force airstrike killed at least 100 villagers in Pazigyi.
William III and Mary II were crowned joint sovereigns of England in a ceremony at Westminster Abbey.

image.caption: King of England , Scotland , and Ireland ( more... )

facts.text: Napoleonic Wars: A hastily assembled Royal Navy fleet launched an assault against the main strength of the French Atlantic Fleet; an incomplete victory led to political turmoil in Britain.
U.S. president Harry S. Truman relieved General of the Army Douglas MacArthur of his commands for making public statements about the Korean War that contradicted the administration's policies.
In a FIFA World Cup qualifying match, Australia defeated American Samoa 31–0, the largest margin of victory recorded in international football.
American Revolution: The North Carolina Provincial Congress passed the Halifax Resolves, the first official action in the American colonies calling for independence from Great Britain.
The Froberg mutiny of Greek and Albanian troops in British service ended with the explosion of the gunpowder magazine at Fort Ricasoli, Malta.
Greek War of Independence: Ottoman troops began a massacre of tens of thousands of Greeks (depicted) on the island of Chios.
The Broughton Suspension Bridge near Manchester, England, collapsed reportedly because of mechanical resonance induced by troops marching in step across it.
Confederate forces began a bombardment of Fort Sumter in the harbor of Charleston, South Carolina, starting the American Civil War.
Aboard Vostok 1, Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin performed the first human spaceflight, completing one orbit of Earth in 108 minutes.
About 1,700 gravediggers in New York City began a 12-week strike, causing a delay in the burial of roughly 1,400 bodies in the city.
Canadian athlete Terry Fox embarked on an east-to-west "Marathon of Hope" from St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador, with a prosthetic leg to raise funds for cancer research.
Harold Washington was elected as the first African-American mayor of Chicago.
Bosnian War: NATO forces began Operation Deny Flight to enforce a no-fly zone over Bosnia and Herzegovina ordered by the United Nations Security Council.

image.caption: Date 12 April 1993 – 20 December 1995; (2 years, 8 months, 1 week, and 1 day) Location Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia Result Inconclusive

facts.text: The Guinea-Bissau military seized control in a coup amid a presidential election, later handing power to a transitional administration under Manuel Serifo Nhamadjo.
Four Chadian soldiers were killed in a suicide bombing by jihadist rebels in Kidal, Mali.
King Edwin of Northumbria was baptised by Bishop Paulinus of York.
Troops of the Fourth Crusade entered Constantinople and began a sack of the city, temporarily dissolving the Byzantine Empire.
SMS Zrínyi, one of the last pre-dreadnoughts built by the Austro-Hungarian Navy, was launched in Trieste.
Samuel Doe took control of Liberia in a coup d'état, overthrowing President William Tolbert and ending over 130 years of national democratic presidential succession.
A fire broke out near Valparaíso, Chile, eventually destroying at least 2,500 homes and leaving approximately 11,000 people homeless.
The first performance of George Frideric Handel 's celebrated oratorio Messiah took place in Dublin.
During a closed session of the Diet of Hungary, Lajos Kossuth presented the Hungarian Declaration of Independence from the Habsburg monarchy.
Austrian soldier Anton Schmid was executed for rescuing Jews from the Ponary massacre in Vilnius.
The Neoclassical Jefferson Memorial in Washington, D.C., was formally dedicated on the 200th anniversary of Thomas Jefferson 's birth.

image.caption: Location of Jefferson Memorial in central Washington, D.C. Show map of Central Washington, D.C. Location within the United States Show map of the United States

facts.text: Nakam, a Jewish organization seeking revenge for the Holocaust, attempted to poison thousands of SS prisoners at Langwasser internment camp, but did not kill anyone.
Ian Fleming 's novel Casino Royale was published as the first work to feature the British spy character James Bond.
The CIA began Project MKUltra, an illegal, covert human research program into mind control.
The Vietnamese National Army captured Ba Cụt, a military commander of the religious sect Hòa Hảo, which ran a de facto state in South Vietnam in opposition to Prime Minister Ngô Đình Diệm.
Catch a Fire, the landmark reggae album by Bob Marley and the Wailers, was released.
Forty people died in an explosion at an ammunition factory in Lapua, Finland.
In golf, 21-year-old Tiger Woods became the youngest player to win the Masters Tournament, breaking the record for the lowest four-round score.
Twenty-three people died in a fire at a homeless hostel in Kamień Pomorski; it was Poland's deadliest fire since 1980.
American Revolutionary War: British and Hessian forces conducted a surprise attack against a Continental Army outpost at Bound Brook, New Jersey.
The Roman Catholic Relief Act received royal assent, removing the most substantial restrictions on Catholics in the United Kingdom.

links.title: Catholic Church in the United Kingdom

facts.text: In the midst of the Cold War, American pianist Van Cliburn won the inaugural International Tchaikovsky Competition in Moscow.

image.caption: Born Harvey Lavan Cliburn Jr. ( 1934-07-12 ) July 12, 1934 Shreveport, Louisiana , U.S.

facts.text: Andrew Hussie 's webcomic Homestuck debuted, and concluded on the same day in 2016.
War in Afghanistan: In an airstrike in Nangarhar Province, the U.S. military dropped the most powerful conventional bomb used in combat.
Polish ruler Mieszko I converted to Christianity, an event considered to be the founding of the Polish state.

links.title: History of Poland during the Piast dynasty

facts.text: Lexicographer Noah Webster copyrighted the first edition of his dictionary of American English
Actor and Confederate sympathizer John Wilkes Booth fatally shot U.S. president Abraham Lincoln at Ford's Theatre in Washington, D.C.
The Azusa Street Revival, the primary catalyst for the spread of Pentecostalism in the 20th century, opened in Los Angeles.
The first Hauser Dam in the U.S. state of Montana failed, causing severe flooding and damage downstream.
Following a reactionary military revolt against the Committee of Union and Progress, a mob began a massacre of Armenian Christians in the Adana Vilayet of the Ottoman Empire.
Dust Bowl: A severe dust storm swept across Oklahoma and northern Texas, removing an estimated 300 million tons of topsoil from the prairies.
The freighter Fort Stikine, carrying cotton bales, gold and ammunition, exploded in the harbour of Bombay, India, sinking surrounding ships and causing about 800 deaths.
After leading a military coup three months earlier, Gnassingbé Eyadéma installed himself as President of Togo, a post that he held until 2005.

After an oxygen tank aboard Apollo 13 exploded, disabling the spacecraft's electrical and life-support systems, astronaut Jack Swigert reported: " Houston, we've had a problem here " (audio featured).
Thousands of Georgians demonstrated in Tbilisi against an attempt by the Supreme Soviet of the Georgian SSR to change the constitutional status of the Georgian language.
Let's Dance, English musician David Bowie 's best-selling album, was released.

Iraqi no-fly zones conflict: In a friendly-fire incident during Operation Provide Comfort, two U.S. Air Force aircraft mistakenly shot down two U.S. Army helicopters over northern Iraq, killing 26 people.
Plumes of ash from a major eruption of the Eyjafjallajökull volcano in Iceland led to widespread disruption of air travel throughout Europe for several days.

links.title: Air travel disruption after the 2010 Eyjafjallajökull eruption

facts.text: Nearly 2,700 people were killed in an earthquake registering 6.9 M w in Yushu Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, China.
Western Kentucky University announced a five-year suspension of their swimming and diving programs as a result of a hazing scandal.

links.title: Western Kentucky University swim team hazing scandal

facts.text: Wars of the Roses: The Yorkists under Edward IV defeated the Lancastrians at the Battle of Barnet, killing Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick.
World War II: The German town of Friesoythe was razed by the 4th Canadian Division on the orders of Major General Christopher Vokes.

A storm dropped around 500,000 tonnes of hailstones on Sydney and the east coast of New South Wales, causing about A$ 2.3 billion in damages, the costliest natural disaster in Australian insurance history.
Boko Haram militants kidnapped 276 schoolgirls from a government secondary school in the town of Chibok, Nigeria.
The final session of the Lateran Council, convened to rectify abuses in the papal electoral process that had led to the elevation of the antipopes Constantine II and Philip, was held in Rome.

Byzantine–Norman wars: After a siege of almost three years, Italo-Norman forces conquered the city of Bari, the capital of the Catepanate of Italy, ending more than five centuries of Byzantine presence in the region.
Serse, an opera by Baroque composer George Frideric Handel loosely based on Xerxes I of Persia, premiered in London.

English poet William Wordsworth and his sister Dorothy encountered a "long belt" of daffodils while walking around Ullswater in the Lake District, inspiring him to pen his best-known work, " I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud ".

links.title: I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud

facts.text: At the start of the American Civil War, president Abraham Lincoln calls for 75,000 volunteers to quell an insurrection following the bombardment of Fort Sumter.
More than 1,500 people on the Titanic died when the passenger liner sank after colliding with an iceberg southeast of Newfoundland.

U.S. senator John B. Kendrick introduced a resolution calling for an investigation of a secret land deal involving U.S. president Warren G. Harding 's administration, leading to the Teapot Dome scandal.
Torrential rains caused the Mississippi River to break out of its levee system in at least 145 places, resulting in the worst flooding in the history of the United States.
Jackie Robinson, the first African American to break the baseball color line, played his first game in Major League Baseball.
The Boeing B-52 Stratofortress, a long-range, subsonic, jet-powered, strategic bomber operated by the U.S. Air Force for most of the aircraft's history, made its first flight.
The Indiaman departed Victoria Coach Station, London, as part of the first UK–India bus service.
On Walter O'Malley 's initiative, the Los Angeles Dodgers and San Francisco Giants played the first Major League Baseball game on the U.S. West Coast.
At a GATT ministerial meeting in Marrakesh, Morocco, representatives of 123 countries and the European Communities signed an agreement to establish the World Trade Organization.

links.title: General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade

facts.text: Dzhokhar and Tamerlan Tsarnaev set off two pressure cooker bombs during the running of the Boston Marathon, killing three people and injuring 264 others.
Thirty Years' War: A Swedish–German army defeated the forces of the Catholic League at the Battle of Rain, mortally wounding their commander Johann Tserclaes, Count of Tilly.
Ten Japanese-American children were killed in a racially motivated arson attack on a school in Sacramento, California.
Two Jews were killed near Tulkarm in Mandatory Palestine, an act widely viewed as the beginning of violence within the Arab revolt.
The Hillsborough disaster, a human crush that caused 97 deaths in the worst disaster in British sporting history, occurred during an FA Cup match between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest in Sheffield.

image.caption: Hillsborough Stadium Hillsborough Stadium in Sheffield

facts.text: A fire severely damaged Notre-Dame de Paris, destroying the cathedral's timber spire and much of the roof.
French Revolutionary Wars: Severely outnumbered French forces repulsed an Ottoman attack at the Battle of Mount Tabor in present-day Israel.
American pilot Harriet Quimby became the first woman to fly across the English Channel.

image.caption: Born ( 1875-05-21 ) May 21, 1875 Arcadia, Michigan , US

facts.text: World War I: Several French army corps began a massive assault against the German-occupied Chemin des Dames ridge, south of Laon, France.
Polish–Soviet War: The Polish army launched the Vilna offensive to capture Vilnius (now in Lithuania) from the Red Army.
In response to an open letter written by white clergymen, Martin Luther King Jr. wrote the Letter from Birmingham Jail in defence of the strategy of nonviolent resistance against racism.
India and Bangladesh began a six-day conflict over their disputed border, which ended in a stalemate.

In one of the deadliest shooting incidents in United States history, a gunman killed 32 people and wounded over 20 more before committing suicide at the Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University in Blacksburg, Virginia.

image.caption: 220m 240yds 2 Norris Hall 1 Ambler Johnston Hall

links.title: Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University

facts.text: A revolt of citizens in Toledo, Castile, opposed to the rule of the foreign-born Charles I began when the royal government attempted to unseat radical city councilors.
Slavery in Washington, D.C., ended when the District of Columbia Compensated Emancipation Act became law.

links.title: District of Columbia Compensated Emancipation Act

facts.text: Second World War: British and Canadian forces concluded the Liberation of Arnhem in the Netherlands from German occupation.
The Organisation for European Economic Co-operation, headquartered in Paris, was founded.
The ferry MV Sewol capsized and sank off Donggeochado, South Korea, killing 306 people, mainly students from Danwon High School.
Lithuanian Crusade: After a month-long siege, forces of the Teutonic Order captured and destroyed Kaunas Castle, which was defended by troops of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania.

image.caption: Date March 13 – April 17, 1362 Location Kaunas Castle 54°53′56″N 23°53′6″E ﻿ / ﻿ 54.89889°N 23.88500°E ﻿ / 54.89889; 23.88500 Result Teutonic victory

facts.text: The Mechanical Turk, a fraudulent chess -playing "machine" by Wolfgang von Kempelen that was secretly controlled by a hidden human, began a tour of Europe.
French Revolutionary Wars: British forces commanded by Lieutenant-General Ralph Abercromby invaded the Spanish colonial port of San Juan, Puerto Rico.
Minas Geraes, the first of three Brazilian dreadnought battleships, was laid down, sparking a vastly expensive South American naval arms race with Argentina and Chile.
Sirhan Sirhan was convicted of the assassination of United States Senator Robert F. Kennedy.
Ustaše -affiliated Croatian separatists attacked the Yugoslav embassy in Stockholm, fatally shooting the ambassador, Vladimir Rolović.
George Lucas began writing a 13-page film treatment that later formed the basis of Star Wars.

Metropolitan Police officer Yvonne Fletcher was shot and killed while on duty during a protest outside the Libyan embassy in London, resulting in an 11-day police siege of the building and a breakdown of Libya–United Kingdom relations.
Having supposedly been at war for 335 years without a single shot having been fired and no casualties incurred, the Netherlands and the Isles of Scilly declared peace.

links.title: Three Hundred and Thirty Five Years' War

facts.text: Canute IV became King of Denmark upon the death of his brother Harald III.
Napoleonic Wars: After a three-day chase, the French ship D'Hautpoul was captured off Puerto Rico by a British squadron under Alexander Cochrane.
The Peak District was designated the first national park in the United Kingdom.

links.title: National parks of the United Kingdom

facts.text: The Khmer Rouge captured Phnom Penh, the capital of the Khmer Republic, ending the Cambodian Civil War and establishing the socialist state of Democratic Kampuchea.
NASA announced the discovery of Kepler-186f, the first exoplanet with a radius similar to Earth's discovered in the habitable zone of another star.

image.caption: Discovery [ 1 ]

facts.text: Glorious Revolution: Provincial militia and citizens in Boston revolted, arresting officials of the Dominion of New England.
American Civil War: African-American Union soldiers were massacred and mutilated during and after the Battle of Poison Spring.
Superman, created by Jerry Siegel and Joe Shuster of DC Comics, made his debut in Action Comics #1, the first true superhero comic book.
The final session of the League of Nations concluded in Geneva, with delegates agreeing to transfer much of its assets to the United Nations.
Controversial American poet Ezra Pound was released from St. Elizabeths Hospital, a psychiatric hospital in Washington, D.C., in which he had been incarcerated for twelve years.
Robert Mugabe became the first prime minister of Zimbabwe, beginning a 37-year period in power.
Operation Grapes of Wrath: Israeli forces shelled Qana, Lebanon, killing at least 100 civilians and injuring more than 110 others at a United Nations compound.

links.title: United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon

facts.text: A ladle spilled 30 tonnes (33 tons) of molten steel in a factory in Liaoning, China, killing 32 workers.
The United States Department of Justice released a redacted version of the Mueller report about the investigation of Russian influence on the U.S. presidential election to Congress and the public.

American Revolutionary War: Colonists Paul Revere and William Dawes, later joined by Samuel Prescott, began a midnight ride to warn residents of Lexington and Concord, Massachusetts, about the impending arrival of British troops.
The painted ceilings of the Natural History Museum, London, were unveiled when the building opened its doors to the public.

links.title: Ceilings of the Natural History Museum, London

facts.text: World War I: Hit by ground fire, French aviation pioneer Roland Garros landed his aircraft behind enemy lines and was taken prisoner by German forces.

image.caption: Born Eugène Adrien Roland Georges Garros [ 1 ] ( 1888-10-06 ) 6 October 1888 Saint-Denis, Réunion , France

facts.text: The Republic of Ireland Act 1948 came into force, describing Ireland as a republic and ending its membership in the Commonwealth of Nations.
Aryabhata, India's first satellite, was launched from Kapustin Yar in the Soviet Union.
In Lisbon, a crowd began a massacre of Jews who had been forced to convert to Christianity.
The Polish Partition Sejm met to discuss the First Partition of Poland, carried out the previous year by Russia, Prussia and Austria.
The American Revolutionary War began with the Battles of Lexington and Concord in the British colony of Massachusetts.
The States General of the Dutch Republic received John Adams, and the house he had purchased in The Hague became the first United States embassy.

links.title: List of diplomatic missions of the United States

facts.text: Anti-Jewish riots broke out in Kishinev, the capital of Bessarabia Governorate, causing the death of nearly 50 Jews and focusing worldwide attention on the persecution of Jews in Russia.
American actress Mae West was sentenced to ten days in jail for "corrupting the morals of youth" with her play Sex.

image.caption: Born Mary Jane West ( 1893-08-17 ) August 17, 1893 Brooklyn , New York , U.S.

facts.text: American actress Grace Kelly became the princess consort of Monaco upon her marriage to Rainier III.

image.caption: Princess consort of Monaco

facts.text: Salyut 1, the first space station, was launched from the Baikonur Cosmodrome near Tyuratam in the Soviet Union.
The Doors ' L.A. Woman was released, their final album during Jim Morrison 's lifetime.
" Advance Australia Fair ", written by Scottish-born composer Peter Dodds McCormick, officially replaced " God Save the Queen " as Australia's national anthem.
A gun turret exploded on board the United States Navy battleship Iowa, killing 47 sailors.
With no living male heirs, Charles VI, Holy Roman Emperor, issued the Pragmatic Sanction, allowing the Habsburg hereditary possessions to be inherited by a daughter.
War of the Fifth Coalition: French general Louis-Nicolas Davout defeated an Austrian force in Lower Bavaria, allowing him to rejoin the main French army.
The Minute Man is unveiled as part of the centennial celebration of the Battles of Lexington and Concord.
The fictional Simpson family made their first appearance in the short " Good Night ", aired in a segment of the The Tracey Ullman Show.
A truck bombing destroyed much of the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building in Oklahoma City, killing 168 people and injuring more than 680 others.

image.caption: Location 35°28′22″N 97°31′01″W ﻿ / ﻿ 35.47278°N 97.51694°W ﻿ / 35.47278; -97.51694 Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building Oklahoma City , Oklahoma, U.S.

facts.text: Freddie Gray, a 25-year-old African American, died of injuries sustained while in the custody of the Baltimore Police Department.
Bacatá, the main settlement of the Muisca Confederation in present-day Colombia, was conquered by Spanish conquistadors led by Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada.
War of the Fifth Coalition: Commanded by Napoleon, Franco-German forces defeated a reinforced Austrian corps at the Battle of Abensberg.
Four days after the Court of King's Bench upheld an English murder suspect's right to a trial by battle in Ashford v Thornton, the plaintiff declined to fight, allowing the defendant to go free.

French explorer René Caillié reached Timbuktu in present-day Mali, and later received a 9,000- franc prize from the Société de Géographie for being the first European to return with a description of the city.
A fire and a gun battle between the Colorado National Guard and striking coal miners led to 17 deaths in the Ludlow Massacre.
Adolf Hitler's 50th birthday was celebrated as a national holiday in Nazi Germany.
Billie Holiday recorded the song " Strange Fruit ", which later became an emblem of the civil rights movement.
World War II: German and Italian forces began a large-scale counter-insurgency operation in occupied Yugoslavia.

Enoch Powell, a British Conservative member of Parliament, made a controversial speech in opposition to immigration and anti-discrimination legislation, resulting in his removal from the shadow cabinet.
South African Airways Flight 228 crashed shortly after take-off from Windhoek in South West Africa, resulting in 123 deaths.
Korean Air Lines Flight 902 was shot down after violating Soviet airspace and was forced to make an emergency landing.
Students Eric Harris and Dylan Klebold carried out a massacre at Columbine High School, killing 13 people before committing suicide.
American racing driver Danica Patrick won the Indy Japan 300, becoming the first woman to win an IndyCar auto race.
Fernando Lugo became the first candidate not from the Colorado Party candidate to be elected President of Paraguay in 61 years.
Sun dogs were observed over Stockholm, Sweden, inspiring Vädersolstavlan, the oldest coloured depiction of the city.

image.caption: Artist Urban målare , Jacob Elbfas

facts.text: Anglo-Spanish War: The English navy sank much of a Spanish treasure fleet at the Battle of Santa Cruz de Tenerife off the Canary Islands, but was unable to capture the treasure.

links.title: Battle of Santa Cruz de Tenerife (1657)

facts.text: Pierre Trudeau was sworn in as prime minister of Canada, succeeding Lester B. Pearson.
An incomplete tunnel leading to the Nicoll Highway MRT station in Singapore collapsed, resulting in four deaths and the station's relocation.
An explosion on Deepwater Horizon, an offshore rig in the Gulf of Mexico, resulted in the largest marine oil spill in history.
Ælfric of Abingdon was appointed Archbishop of Canterbury
The Ladies of Trenton social club hosted a reception (depicted) for President-elect George Washington as he journeyed to New York City for his first inauguration.
The "Surgeon's Photograph", purportedly showing the Loch Ness Monster (later revealed to be a hoax), was published in the Daily Mail.

Forces of the Republic of Texas led by Sam Houston defeated the Mexican troops of General Antonio López de Santa Anna in the Battle of San Jacinto, the decisive and final battle of the Texas Revolution.
United Airlines Flight 736 collided with a U.S. Air Force fighter jet over southern Nevada, resulting in the deaths of all 49 people on board both aircraft.
The Century 21 Exposition, the first world's fair in the United States since World War II, opened in Seattle.
A violent tornado strikes multiple schools and destroys houses in Belvidere, Illinois, United States, causing over 450 casualties.
In response to a dispute over wheat production quotas, Leonard Casley declared his 75 km 2 (29 sq mi) farm in Western Australia to be an independent country as the Hutt River Province.
Ukraine and Russia signed the Kharkiv Pact, extending the Russian lease on naval facilities in Crimea.
The city of Flint, Michigan, U.S., changed its water source to the Flint River, which exposed residents to lead poisoning.
The Indonesian Navy submarine Nanggala sank, resulting in the deaths of all 53 people on board.
A debt was pardoned by the chief of Tondo on the island of Luzon and recorded on the Laguna Copperplate Inscription, the earliest known calendar-dated document found in the Philippines.
The Wignacourt Aqueduct in Malta was inaugurated, and was used to carry water to Valletta for about 300 years.
J. S. Bach 's cantata Bleib bei uns, denn es will Abend werden, was first performed on Easter Monday.

links.title: Bleib bei uns, denn es will Abend werden, BWV 6

facts.text: South Vietnamese president Nguyễn Văn Thiệu resigned on hearing of the fall of Xuân Lộc, the last battle of the Vietnam War.
Henry VIII became King of England, following the death of his father Henry VII, eventually becoming a significant figure in the history of the English monarchy.
The U.S. Congress authorized the creation of a two-cent coin, the first U.S. currency to bear the phrase " In God We Trust ".

image.caption: Design Shield, "IN GOD WE TRUST" on banner, date below.

facts.text: About 600 prisoners of the Jasenovac concentration camp in the Independent State of Croatia revolted, but only 80 managed to escape while the remainder were killed by the Ustaše regime.
Civil War in Mandatory Palestine: The Jewish paramilitary group Haganah captured Haifa from the Arab Liberation Army.

Stephen Lawrence, a black British teenager, was murdered while waiting for a bus in Eltham, London, leading to cultural changes of attitudes on racism and the police, and to the law and police practice.
In a pre-dawn raid, U.S. federal agents seized six-year-old Elián González from his relatives' home in Miami and returned him to his Cuban father.
Flammable cargo exploded at a railway station in Ryongchon, North Korea, killing at least 54 people and injuring more than a thousand others.
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police arrested two men who were plotting to commit terrorist attacks against Via Rail operations.
American climate activist Wynn Bruce set himself on fire outside the United States Supreme Court Building in an apparent protest against the climate crisis.
A fleet commanded by Pedro Álvares Cabral anchored off present-day Brazil; he later claimed the land for the Portuguese Empire.

image.caption: Born Pedro Álvares de Gouveia 1467 or 1468 Belmonte , Kingdom of Portugal

facts.text: The first meeting of the Colonial Defence Committee, a standing committee of the British Colonial Office, was held to discuss the defence of Barbados.
The short-lived Transcaucasian Democratic Federative Republic was established on territory formerly part of the Russian Empire.
Korean War: The Chinese People's Volunteer Army attacked positions occupied mainly by Australian and Canadian forces, starting the Battle of Kapyong.
The Paris Agreement, an international treaty on climate change, opened for signature and was signed by 175 parties.

links.title: List of parties to the Paris Agreement

facts.text: The Vikings were defeated by the Irish at the Battle of Clontarf.
The first knights of the Order of the Garter, an order of chivalry founded by King Edward III of England, were appointed.
Albanian commander Skanderbeg entered Krujë, breaking a 10-month siege by Ottoman forces.
Charles II was crowned King of England, Scotland and Ireland at Westminster Abbey.
Succeeding Charles II, his late brother, James II was crowned King of England, becoming last Catholic to hold the title.
Johann Sebastian Bach leads the first performance of his cantata Du Hirte Israel, höre, BWV 104, illustrating the topic of the Good Shepherd in pastoral music.
Chilean Civil War: The armored frigate Blanco Encalada was sunk at the Battle of Caldera Bay, the first ironclad warship lost to a self-propelled torpedo.
First World War: The British Royal Navy launched unsuccessful raids on Ostend and Zeebrugge in German-occupied Belgium.
The Grand National Assembly of Turkey, the country's unicameral legislature, first met in Ankara in the midst of the Turkish War of Independence.
Cardiff City defeated Arsenal 1–0 in the FA Cup final in the only time the FA Cup has been won by a non-English team.

image.caption: Event 1926–27 FA Cup

facts.text: Second World War: In retaliation for the Royal Air Force 's bombing of Lübeck, the Luftwaffe began a series of air raids across England, beginning with Exeter.

links.title: Bombing of Lübeck in World War II

facts.text: American journalist William N. Oatis was arrested for espionage by the communist government of Czechoslovakia.
Batting for the Milwaukee Braves against Vic Raschi of the St. Louis Cardinals, Hank Aaron hit the first of his 755 home runs in Major League Baseball.
The Rolling Stones released Sticky Fingers, the first album on their own label, Rolling Stones Records.
The gamma-ray burst GRB 090423 was detected coming from the most distant astronomical object of any kind known at the time.

links.title: List of the most distant astronomical objects

facts.text: Arizona governor Jan Brewer signed into law the controversial anti– illegal immigration bill SB 1070, much of which was later struck down by the U.S. Supreme Court.
A landslide triggered the collapse of a jade mine in Hpakant, Myanmar, resulting in six confirmed deaths and presumed dozens more.
Ottoman wars in Europe: Albanian leader Skanderbeg defeated an Ottoman army under Ballaban Badera to raise the siege of Krujë.
World War II: The US Army's 90th Infantry Division liberated Flossenbürg concentration camp in Germany, freeing 1,500 prisoners.

image.caption: Interactive map of Flossenbürg

facts.text: The American band the Ramones released their debut album, which became highly influential on the emerging punk rock movement.
Blair Peach, a New Zealand teacher, was fatally injured while taking part in an Anti-Nazi League demonstration against a National Front election meeting in Southall, London.
A man intentionally struck pedestrians with a van on Yonge Street in Toronto, Canada, leading to 11 deaths.
John Campbell released the first issue of The Boston News-Letter, the first continuously published newspaper in British North America.

The Library of Congress, the de facto national library of the United States, was established as part of an act of Congress providing for the transfer of the nation's capital from Philadelphia to Washington, D.C.

image.caption: Main reading room in the Thomas Jefferson Building at the Library of Congress

facts.text: German composer Max Bruch conducted the premiere of his first violin concerto, which later became his most famous work.
Realizing that the Russification of Lithuania was not working, the Russian Empire lifted the 40-year-old ban on publications written in Lithuanian language using the Latin alphabet.
The Woolworth Building in New York City officially opened; at the time, it was the tallest building in the world, with a height of 792 ft (241 m).
The Armenian Genocide in the Ottoman Empire began with the arrest and deportation of hundreds of prominent Armenians in Constantinople.

links.title: Deportation of Armenian intellectuals on 24 April 1915

facts.text: First World War: The Second Battle of Villers-Bretonneux began, which contained the first instance of tanks fighting against each other.
The first portion of the Imperial Wireless Chain, a strategic international wireless telegraphy communications network created to link the countries of the British Empire, opened.
An estimated 400 ramblers committed a wilful mass trespass of Kinder Scout in the Peak District to highlight the denial of access to areas of open country in England.

image.caption: Date 24 April 1932 ; 93 years ago ( 1932-04-24 )

facts.text: Nazi Germany began its persecution of Jehovah's Witnesses by shutting down the Watch Tower Society office in Magdeburg.

links.title: Persecution of Jehovah's Witnesses in Nazi Germany

facts.text: World War II: The British Special Boat Service executed a successful raid to destroy an Axis radio station on the Greek island of Santorini.
Cold War: The Dominican Civil War broke out due to tensions following a military coup against the democratically elected government of President Juan Bosch two years earlier.
Eight U.S. servicemen died in Operation Eagle Claw, a failed attempt to rescue the captives in the Iran hostage crisis.
A backhoe breached a pipeline in Toronto, Canada, which caused a gas explosion that killed seven people.
Secret documents relating to detainees at the United States' Guantanamo Bay detention camp were released on WikiLeaks and several independent news organizations.
A building in the Savar Upazila of Dhaka, Bangladesh, collapsed, killing 1,134 people, making it the deadliest accidental structural failure in modern history.
A fire broke out in Surat, India, which went on to destroy about 75% of the city.
The Franck–Hertz experiment, the first electrical measurement to clearly demonstrate quantum mechanics, was presented to the German Physical Society.
Irish republicans led by Patrick Pearse began the Easter Rising against British rule in Ireland, and proclaimed the Irish Republic an independent state.
The Hubble Space Telescope was launched aboard STS-31 by Space Shuttle Discovery.

The Provisional Irish Republican Army detonated a truck bomb in London's financial district in Bishopsgate, killing one person, injuring forty-four others, and causing damage that cost £350 million to repair.
The Abbasid army won a decisive victory over the forces of rebelling Armenian princes at the Battle of Bagrevand.
Pope Leo III was attacked by partisans of his predecessor Adrian I, but was rescued and taken to Charlemagne, as described in the epic Karolus magnus et Leo papa.
Ming–Qing transition: The Ming dynasty of China fell when the Chongzhen Emperor committed suicide during a peasant rebellion led by Li Zicheng.
At the San Remo conference, the principal Allies of World War I passed a resolution allocating League of Nations mandates for the administration of former Ottoman territories in the Middle East.
A march by blind people from across the United Kingdom to protest at poor working conditions ended at Trafalgar Square, London.
Gladys Elinor Watkins consecrated the carillon of the National War Memorial in Wellington, New Zealand.

image.caption: Born ( 1884-10-20 ) 20 October 1884 Akaroa , New Zealand

facts.text: Two passenger trains collided in Naperville, Illinois, leaving 45 people dead and some 125 injured.
109 individuals were arrested in a police raid on a gay bar near Chicago.
British prime minister Margaret Thatcher told journalists in Downing Street to " rejoice " upon hearing news of the successful recapture of South Georgia from Argentine forces in the Falklands War.
Violeta Chamorro took office as President of Nicaragua, becoming the first female head of state in the Americas to have been elected in her own right.
First English Civil War: Despite being vastly outnumbered, a Parliamentarian force under James Chudleigh defeated a Royalist army near Okehampton, Devon, at the Battle of Sourton Down.

First World War: The Australian and New Zealand Army Corps landed at Anzac Cove while British and French troops landed at Cape Helles to begin the Allied invasion of the Gallipoli peninsula in the Ottoman Empire.

links.title: Australian and New Zealand Army Corps

facts.text: The first issue of Irish War News was published in Ireland.
The U.S. Navy submarine Triton completed the first submerged circumnavigation of the world.
The first issue of The Jakarta Post was published in Indonesia.
Nepal was struck by a magnitude-7.8 earthquake, killing more than 8,000 people.
U.S. Army soldiers cornered and fatally shot John Wilkes Booth, the assassin of U.S. president Abraham Lincoln, ending a twelve-day manhunt.
Boris Kidrič and Edvard Kardelj founded the Liberation Front of the Slovene Nation, the main anti-fascist Slovene civil-resistance and political organization during World War II.

links.title: Liberation Front of the Slovene Nation

facts.text: World War II: U.S. Navy submarines began attacks on Japan's Take Ichi convoy as it sailed in waters between Taiwan and the Philippines, eventually sinking four vessels and killing more than 4,000 troops.
Service ended on the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad 's Royal Blue Line, one of the first major electrified train lines in the U.S..

image.caption: Overview

facts.text: The World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) came into being when the WIPO Convention entered into force.
An editorial was published in the People's Daily denouncing the growing unrest in Tiananmen Square in Beijing which would remain contentious through the remainder of the protests.
Controversy surrounding the relocation of the Bronze Soldier of Tallinn, a Soviet Red Army World War II memorial in Tallinn, Estonia, erupted into mass protests and riots.
The International Hydrographic Organization abandoned South Korean-led ' attempts to rename the Sea of Japan.
In a conspiracy to replace the Medici family as rulers of the Republic of Florence, the Pazzi family attacked Lorenzo de' Medici and killed his brother Giuliano at Florence Cathedral.
First World War: Britain, France and Russia signed a secret treaty promising territory to Italy if it joined the war on their side.
The Gestapo, the official secret police force of Nazi Germany, was established.
A tornado struck the Manikganj District of Bangladesh and killed an estimated 1,300 people, making it the deadliest tornado in history.

Just before landing at Nagoya Airport, Japan, the copilot of China Airlines Flight 140 inadvertently triggered the takeoff/go-around switch, causing the aircraft to crash and killing 264 of the 271 people on board.
Aelia Eudoxia married Byzantine emperor Arcadius without the knowledge or consent of Rufinus, the Praetorian prefect who had intended for his own daughter to wed the emperor.
Filipino natives led by chieftain Lapulapu killed Portuguese explorer Ferdinand Magellan at the Battle of Mactan.
Four Years' War: The combined forces of Spain and the Papal States defeated a French and Venetian army at the Battle of Bicocca.
American Revolutionary War: British Army regulars defeated Patriot militias in the Battle of Ridgefield, galvanizing resistance in the Connecticut Colony.

links.title: British soldiers in the eighteenth century

facts.text: Ludwig van Beethoven composed his Bagatelle No. 25 in A minor, better known as " Für Elise ", one of his most popular compositions.
The French National Assembly under Victor Schœlcher proclaims the abolition of slavery within France and it's colonies following the February Revolution.
Chris Watson became the first prime minister of Australia from the Australian Labor Party.
In response to the treatment of Lorenzo Gamboa under the White Australia policy, the Philippine House of Representatives passed a bill banning Australians from the country.
Prime Minister Milton Margai led the Sierra Leone Colony and Protectorate to independence from the United Kingdom.
The Expo 67 world's fair opened in Montreal, with 62 nations participating and more than 50 million visitors ultimately attending.
The black-ball final, one of the most famous snooker matches in history, began between Steve Davis and Dennis Taylor.
Unknown perpetrators carried out a series of four bombings in Dnipropetrovsk, Ukraine.
Shahrbaraz usurped the throne of the Sasanian Empire from Ardashir III, but was himself killed six weeks later.
Wars of the Three Kingdoms: Covenanter forces defeated the Royalists at the Battle of Carbisdale near the village of Culrain, Scotland.
World War II: The photograph Raising the Flag on the Three-Country Cairn was taken after German troops withdrew to Norway at the end of the Lapland War.

links.title: Raising the Flag on the Three-Country Cairn

facts.text: Indonesia–Malaysia confrontation: British forces repelled a surprise Indonesian attack on a base at Plaman Mapu in Sarawak.
The Airbus A380, the world's largest passenger airliner, made its maiden flight from Toulouse, France.
The ancient Iranian Parthian Empire fell to the Sasanids after its forces were defeated at the Battle of Hormozdgan.
The University of Santo Tomas in Manila, one of the oldest existing universities in Asia and one of the world's largest Catholic universities by enrollment, was founded.
Second Anglo-Mysore War: British troops surrendered the fortress of Bednore in southwestern India to French and Mysorean forces; many of the prisoners were later murdered.
A week after being arrested by the Prussian Secret Police, French police inspector Guillaume Schnaebelé was released on the order of William I, German Emperor, defusing a possible war.
Frenchman Louis Paulhan landed his biplane at Manchester, having departed from London the previous day, to win the world's first long-distance air race
World War II: Presaging a campaign of genocide against the Serbs of Croatia, around 190 people were massacred by members of the Ustaše movement in Gudovac.

links.title: Genocide of Serbs in the Independent State of Croatia

facts.text: Japan and the Republic of China signed the Treaty of Taipei, officially ending the Second Sino-Japanese War seven years after fighting ended due to World War II.
The Sibley Commission issued their final report, urging the government of the U.S. state of Georgia to abandon its strategy of massive resistance and legalize some instances of school integration.

links.title: School integration in the United States

facts.text: Scottish trade unionist Jimmy Reid condemned the capitalist " rat race " in his inaugural address as Rector of the University of Glasgow.

links.title: Rector of the University of Glasgow

facts.text: The album The Dark Side of the Moon by the British progressive rock band Pink Floyd entered the Billboard Top LPs & Tape chart, on which it spent a record 942 weeks.

links.title: The Dark Side of the Moon

facts.text: Aloha Airlines Flight 243 experienced explosive decompression while airborne between Hilo and Honolulu, Hawaii, with one fatality as a flight attendant was ejected from the aircraft.
A 14-year-old former student in Taber, Alberta, opened fire at his high school, killing one student and wounding another in Canada's first fatal school shooting in more than two decades.

links.title: W. R. Myers High School shooting

facts.text: The 1,388-foot-tall (423.2 m) Trump International Hotel and Tower in Chicago, with the world's highest residence above ground level at the time, held its grand opening.
The Japanese monk Nichiren declared the mantra Namu Myōhō Renge Kyō, now a central part of Nichiren Buddhism.
Fletcher Christian, the acting lieutenant on board the Royal Navy ship Bounty, led a mutiny against the commander William Bligh in the South Pacific.
The FA Cup final between Bolton Wanderers and West Ham United was held on the opening day of the Empire Stadium in London.

image.caption: Event 1922–23 FA Cup

facts.text: World War II: Benito Mussolini, the deposed fascist dictator of Italy, was executed by partisans in Giulino.
The West German news magazine Stern published excerpts from the purported diaries of Adolf Hitler, later revealed to be forgeries.
The Grand Duchy of Lithuania decisively won the Battle of the Vikhra River, forcibly making the Principality of Smolensk a vassal state.
In Parramatta, Australia, Scottish astronomer James Dunlop discovered Centaurus A, which was later recognised as one of the nearest radio galaxies to Earth.

image.caption: Observation data ( J2000 epoch )

facts.text: Confederate forts at Grand Gulf survived a bombardment by Union gunboats, preventing Ulysses S. Grant 's troops from crossing the Mississippi River at that point.
A rockslide buried part of the Canadian mining town of Frank under 110 million tonnes of rock, killing around 70 people.
Parliament passed the People's Budget, the first budget in British history with the express intent of redistributing wealth.
After suffering train derailments, defections, and outbreaks of dysentery and typhoid fever which killed two members, the Brazilian football club Santa Cruz returned from their Suicidal Tour.
Second World War: British agent Nancy Wake parachuted into Auvergne, France, becoming a liaison between the Special Operations Executive and the local Maquis group.
The controversial Broadway musical Hair, a product of the counterculture of the 1960s, opened, with its songs becoming anthems of the anti-Vietnam War movement.

links.title: Opposition to United States involvement in the Vietnam War

facts.text: Vietnam War: South Vietnamese forces began the Cambodian campaign, aiming to attack North Vietnamese jungle bases.
Vietnam War: North Vietnam concluded its East Sea Campaign by capturing all of the Spratly Islands held by South Vietnam.
A powerful tropical cyclone struck Chittagong, Bangladesh, killing at least 138,000 people and leaving up to 10 million homeless across the region.
The acquittal of policemen who had beaten African-American motorist Rodney King sparked six days of civil unrest in Los Angeles, during which 63 people were killed.

image.caption: Date April 29 – May 3, 1992 (5 days); 33 years ago

facts.text: The Chemical Weapons Convention entered into force, outlawing the production, stockpiling and use of chemical weapons in the 87 countries that had ratified the convention.

links.title: List of parties to the Chemical Weapons Convention

facts.text: Watched by a worldwide television audience of tens of millions, Prince William and Catherine Middleton were married at Westminster Abbey in London.

links.title: Wedding of Prince William and Catherine Middleton

facts.text: Cyclone Mala made landfall near Thandwe, Myanmar, causing 37 deaths.
Seven Years' War: France began an unsuccessful attempt to retake Quebec City, which had been captured by Britain.

links.title: Battle of the Plains of Abraham

facts.text: On his first voyage, British explorer James Cook and the crew of HMS Endeavour landed at Botany Bay, making the first recorded European landfall on the eastern coast of Australia.
Sixteen-year-old Lilian Salkeld became the first woman to walk from London to Brighton
World War II: The U.S. Army liberated Dachau, the first Nazi concentration camp, and killed German prisoners of war.

Before a crowd of about 165,000 at the Rungrado 1st of May Stadium, Ric Flair and Antonio Inoki competed in the main event of Collision in Korea, the highest attended professional wrestling event of all time.

links.title: List of professional wrestling attendance records

facts.text: The ringleaders of the Bali Nine were executed in Indonesia for attempting to smuggle 8.3 kg (18 lb) of heroin to Australia in 2005.
SN 1006, the brightest supernova in recorded history, first appeared in the constellation Lupus.

image.caption: Event type Supernova , supernova remnant , astronomical radio source , astrophysical X-ray source

facts.text: George Washington took the oath of office as the first president of the United States at Federal Hall in New York City.

links.title: Oath of office of the president of the United States

facts.text: The United States purchased France's claim to the Louisiana Territory for 80 million francs, or less than US$.03 per acre ($.07/ ha ).
New York governor Grover Cleveland signed legislation that led to the creation of Niagara Falls State Park, the United States' first state park.
A crowd of workers, unemployed due to the Panic of 1893, concluded the first significant popular protest march on Washington D.C.
British physicist J. J. Thomson and his team announce the discovery of the electron.
The Federal Industrial Institute for Women opened near Alderson, West Virginia, as the first federal prison for women in the United States.
Douglas Fairbanks and Mary Pickford became the first two celebrities to make imprints of their hands and feet in cement at Grauman's Chinese Theatre in Hollywood, California.

image.caption: Interactive map of Grauman's Chinese Theatre

facts.text: World War II: As Allied forces closed in on Berlin, Nazi leader Adolf Hitler committed suicide in the Führerbunker with Eva Braun one day after their marriage.
Sixteen monks and a nun of the Hindu organisation Ananda Marga were beaten to death and set on fire in Calcutta, India.
Riverdance was performed for the first time, as the interval act for the Eurovision Song Contest.
Faustina Kowalska, a Polish nun whose apparitions of Jesus inspired the Catholic devotion to the Divine Mercy, was canonized by Pope John Paul II.
The New Yorker published an online article and photographs detailing accounts of torture and abuse by American military personnel of Iraqi prisoners held at Abu Ghraib prison in Baghdad.

links.title: Abu Ghraib torture and prisoner abuse

facts.text: A Dutch man drove his car at high speed into a parade in an attempt to kill the Dutch royal family.

links.title: 2009 attack on the Dutch royal family

facts.text: The Diocletianic Persecution of Christians officially ended in the eastern Roman Empire.
Second World War: The Royal Navy submarine HMS Seraph began Operation Mincemeat to deceive Germany about the upcoming invasion of Sicily.
A refusal by the Bristol Omnibus Company and the Transport and General Workers' Union to permit the employment of black bus crews led to a bus boycott in Bristol, England.
American forces completed a helicopter evacuation of U.S. citizens, South Vietnamese civilians and others from Saigon, just before North Vietnamese troops captured the city and ended the Vietnam War.

image.caption: Date 29–30 April 1975 Location Saigon , 17 nautical miles (31 km) from the Vũng Tàu Peninsula Result Successful evacuation

facts.text: A crowd crush killed 45 people during the annual pilgrimage to the tomb of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai in Israel.

links.title: Hillula of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
Tomb of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
